quizzes.stem: A generated tool declares that it reads files, and its code fetches a web page. What does the gate in this module's practice do?

options.a: Approves it, since reading and fetching are both low-risk effects here
options.b: Refuses it, since the proposal never mentioned that effect
options.c: Sends it back for a better description, since the declaration was incomplete
options.d: Holds it for a person to approve, since a fetch is a risky effect

explanation.b: Code that does more than it declared is refused.
explanation.a: Ruled out because the difference is the finding: "the gate compares what the code does with what was declared and refuses the difference".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the finding is a refusal and not a request for a better description: "Compare what the code does with the permissions declared, and refuse the difference".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the network is denied by policy and not held for a person: "The third asks for the network, which the policy denies, so it is refused whatever its code says."

quizzes.stem: A team runs generated tools in a container that has no network access, no secrets and a short lifetime. A colleague says that the code scan is therefore unnecessary. What is the best reply?

options.a: It is a cheap first check for the obvious, and the surroundings hold back the rest
options.b: It is unnecessary only when the container is also given the secrets it needs to work
options.c: It is the real protection, and the container only adds some speed to each run
options.d: It is unnecessary, and the container alone makes generated tools safe whatever their code does

explanation.a: The scan is the cheap first check.
explanation.b: Ruled out because the container holds no secrets: "The lesson for a team that runs generated code itself is the same, and it is a list of absences: no network, no secrets, no shared state, a short life and limits on time and memory."
explanation.c: Ruled out because the scan finds only what its authors thought of: "A scan finds what its authors thought of: a call spelled differently, built from strings or imported by name slips past it."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the scan still does useful work: "The scan is useful for what it does well: it refuses the obvious".

quizzes.stem: In the example, a tool that was approved by the reviewer returns a result without the field that its schema promised. What happens to the result?

options.a: It is passed to the agent with a warning attached to the front of it
options.b: It is filled with a default and passed on to let the run continue
options.c: It is refused before the agent ever sees it
options.d: It is rejected, and the reviewer's approval is withdrawn for every later tool in the run

explanation.c: A result is checked before the agent uses it.
explanation.a: Ruled out because a result that does not match is not passed on: "a result that does not match its schema is rejected before the agent sees it".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the check does not repair data: "Treat the result as data and check it against its schema".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the approval covers one proposal: "the approval covers the proposal that was reviewed and not a later version".

quizzes.stem: A proposal has a forbidden call in its code and a description of a single line. What does the gate decide, and what does the report list?

options.a: A revision request, with the short text as the first problem the gate meets
options.b: A refusal, with the weakness of the text still noted beside it
options.c: An approval behind a gate, with the forbidden call to be removed later in the run
options.d: A refusal, with the findings dropped from the report

explanation.b: A refusal wins and the findings stay in the report.
explanation.a: Ruled out because a refusal comes first: "A refusal comes before a revision, because a fix cannot make a forbidden call acceptable and a revision would invite the agent to try."
explanation.c: Ruled out because the refusal stands: "A proposal with a refusal is refused, whatever else is true of it."
explanation.d: Ruled out because the findings are kept: "The report keeps the findings of a refused proposal, so the agent, and the log, can see everything that was wrong and not only the first thing."

quizzes.stem: A policy allows a timeout of at most 10 seconds, and a proposal asks for exactly 10. What does the gate do?

options.a: Flags it, since a limit should leave some room below it for safety
options.b: Flags it, since only a request below the limit counts as safe to run
options.c: Accepts the figure, since a request that reaches the ceiling has not passed it
options.d: Accepts it, since a person will sign the proposal off afterwards

explanation.a: Ruled out because the margin is not the gate's to add: "the margin belongs in the number that the policy sets".
explanation.b: Ruled out because the value is allowed: "A limit is a number that the policy allows, so a value equal to the limit is allowed."
explanation.d: Ruled out because a timeout within the limit needs no person: "The timeout may equal its limit and the memory may equal its limit, and one second or one megabyte more is flagged."

quizzes.stem: A reviewer approved a tool last week. Today the agent submits a changed version with an added write. What happens?

options.a: It goes through the gate again as a new proposal
options.b: It runs behind a gate if the old version had been gated as well
options.c: It runs, with the approval covering every version of that tool
options.d: It is refused, with a tool allowed to be approved once and never changed

explanation.a: A changed tool is a new proposal.
explanation.c: Ruled out because the approval is not blanket: "An approval belongs to one proposal."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the earlier gating does not carry over: "the person approved what they read and not what the agent might write next".
explanation.d: Ruled out because a changed tool is not forbidden, only reviewed again: "A changed tool is a new proposal and goes through the gate again".

quizzes.stem: Scenario: an agent that writes and proposes its own tools, which a gate reviews before anything runs. A tool's code opens a file for writing, while the proposal declares only reading, and the policy sends writes to a person. What does the gate do?

options.a: Refuses it, since an effect nobody mentioned cannot be approved on its behalf
options.b: Sends it back for a revision of the description, since the declaration is thin
options.c: Approves it behind a gate, since the policy already covers writes
options.d: Approves it outright, since the proposal declares a permission that the policy allows

explanation.c: Ruled out because the gate approves only what was declared: "Its code shows a permission that the proposal did not declare, which is the case of a tool that says it reads and fetches a page."
explanation.b: Ruled out because an undeclared effect is one of the refusals and not a matter of the description: "Three things refuse a proposal." and "Its code shows a permission that the proposal did not declare"
explanation.d: Ruled out because a declared read does not cover the write the code shows: "Its code shows a permission that the proposal did not declare", and a refusal wins: "A proposal with a refusal is refused, whatever else is true of it."

quizzes.stem: Scenario: an agent that writes and proposes its own tools, which a gate reviews before anything runs. A team proposes to run generated tools in a container and to drop the gate, because the container limits the damage. Which gap remains?

options.a: Nothing, because a container makes every tool safe to run
options.b: Nothing checks what the code does against what was declared
options.c: The container's memory limit, which the gate cannot read
options.d: The agent's description of the tool, which a container cannot read

explanation.b: The container holds the run, and only the gate compares the code with its declaration.
explanation.a: Ruled out because a container is only one of the five jobs: "Containment is the environment's job."
explanation.c: Ruled out because the gate reads and flags the limits: "a timeout above the limit and a memory request above the limit".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the gate reads the description: "a gate can require a minimum of words, a name in a fixed form and an example that is valid for the schema".

quizzes.stem: Scenario: an agent that writes and proposes its own tools, which a gate reviews before anything runs. Which record satisfies the audit part of the design?

options.a: A file that the agent keeps and updates for itself after every one of its runs
options.b: A summary that the agent writes by itself at the end of each working day
options.c: One line per run, kept in the folder where the agent saves its tools
options.d: One line per decision and per run, kept where its subject has no access

explanation.d: The audit is kept out of the agent's reach.
explanation.a: Ruled out because an editable file is not an audit: "A log that the agent can edit is not an audit."
explanation.b: Ruled out because a summary by the agent is its own account: "The record has to be written by the gate and the runner and kept where the agent has no write access".
explanation.c: Ruled out because the agent can write where the log is kept: "kept where the agent has no write access".

quizzes.stem: Scenario: an agent that writes and proposes its own tools, which a gate reviews before anything runs. A proposed name is 64 characters of lower-case letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. What does the gate do with the name?

options.a: Flags it, since the longest name has to leave a spare character
options.b: Flags it, because names this long are hard for the model to choose
options.c: Accepts it, as it sits at the ceiling for such labels and not above it
options.d: Accepts it, since the description also has at least 64 words

explanation.a: Ruled out because the length is allowed: "A name may be 64 characters long, and 65 is too long."
explanation.b: Ruled out because the gate checks the form and not the model's taste: "Four things only send it back: a name that is not in the fixed form".
explanation.d: Ruled out because the description has its own minimum: "The description needs at least the minimum number of words, and exactly the minimum is enough."
